cards.q: What is an IPv4 broadcast and what are its two forms?
cards.a: An IPv4 broadcast is traffic addressed to multiple/all hosts within a broadcast domain; it has two forms: directed broadcast (all host bits = 1 for a specific subnet, e.g. 10.1.1.255 for 10.1.1.0/24) and limited broadcast (255.255.255.255, restricted to the local broadcast domain). Broadcasts are normally not routed between IPv4 subnets.

cards.q: What are the differences between a directed and a limited broadcast?
cards.a: A directed broadcast uses host bits all 1 and targets a specific destination subnet, normally not forwarded by routers; the limited broadcast is 255.255.255.255, scoped to the local broadcast domain, and is never routed.

cards.q: How is an IPv4 broadcast carried on Ethernet and where does it remain?
cards.a: On Ethernet it uses the destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF and stays within the Layer 2 broadcast domain, normally a VLAN; a router is normally a broadcast boundary and does not forward IPv4 broadcasts from one subnet to another.

cards.q: What common traffic uses IPv4 broadcast?
cards.a: ARP requests use a Layer 3 broadcast (Ethernet destination FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF); DHCP clients commonly broadcast during initial address acquisition, which a DHCP relay can forward between subnets; and RIPv1 updates use the limited broadcast 255.255.255.255.

cards.q: How do RIPv1 and RIPv2 deliver routing updates?
cards.a: RIPv1 uses the IPv4 limited broadcast 255.255.255.255, while RIPv2 uses the multicast address 224.0.0.9.

cards.q: How do you compute a subnet's directed broadcast address?
cards.a: Set all host bits to 1; for 10.1.1.0/24 the broadcast is 10.1.1.255, and for 10.1.10.64/26 the broadcast is 10.1.10.127 with usable hosts 10.1.10.65–10.1.10.126.
No; the /26 broadcast is 10.1.10.127 because all 6 host bits are set to 1; 10.1.10.79 falls inside the usable host range.

cards.q: For a normal subnet, which two addresses are excluded from hosts and why?
cards.a: The network address (host bits all 0) and the broadcast address (host bits all 1); neither is assigned to an ordinary host, so usable hosts = 2^host_bits − 2, with exceptions for /31 (two usable addresses under RFC 3021) and /32 (single host route with no conventional network/broadcast pair).

cards.q: Do routers forward directed broadcasts by default, and what Cisco command controls this?
cards.a: No; modern Cisco IOS disables directed-broadcast forwarding by default with no ip directed-broadcast on the interface, which helps prevent Smurf attacks that abuse directed broadcasts to amplify ICMP traffic.

cards.q: What is the exam distinction between directed and limited broadcast scope?
cards.a: A directed broadcast can identify a specific remote subnet, but routers normally block forwarding it; the limited broadcast 255.255.255.255 is local-only and is not routed.

cards.q: What is a broadcast storm and how do you control it?
cards.a: A broadcast storm occurs when excessive broadcast traffic consumes network resources, typically from Layer 2 loops, misconfigured devices, excessive ARP/DHCP, or faulty or malicious hosts; controls include STP, storm control, VLAN segmentation, and loop prevention, e.g. the Cisco command storm-control broadcast level 20.

cards.q: What Cisco commands verify or control broadcast behavior?
cards.a: no ip directed-broadcast disables directed-broadcast forwarding on an interface; storm-control broadcast level 20 configures broadcast storm control; show interfaces (or show interfaces | include broadcast) displays broadcast-related interface counters.

cards.q: Does a router ever forward broadcasts?
cards.a: In limited cases, yes: a configured DHCP relay can forward DHCP requests between subnets by converting the L2 broadcast into routed/unicast forwarding, and a router can be explicitly configured to permit directed-broadcast forwarding toward a destination subnet.

cards.q: Does IPv6 use ARP or IPv4-style broadcast?
cards.a: No; IPv6 does not use ARP or IPv4-style broadcasts, instead using Neighbor Discovery (ND) with ICMPv6 multicast.

cards.q: Is every DHCP message always a broadcast?
cards.a: No; DHCP clients commonly use broadcast during initial address acquisition because they lack a usable address and do not know the server, but DHCP messages can also be unicast or relayed, so do not assume every DHCP message is broadcast.

cards.q: State the core IPv4 broadcast facts for the exam.
cards.a: Directed broadcast = host bits all 1 for a specific subnet; limited broadcast = 255.255.255.255; Ethernet broadcast = FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF; routers normally do not forward broadcasts; ARP uses broadcast while IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery; RIPv1 = broadcast 255.255.255.255 and RIPv2 = multicast 224.0.0.9; network address = host bits all 0; normal usable hosts = 2^host_bits − 2.
